_podcast.theme_scoring_prompt:
Rate how well this article fits the theme 'Indigenous Lands & Innovation' — Indigenous nations using technology, governance, and stewardship on their own terms.

OUT OF SCOPE — score 0-9: geopolitical and war news with no Indigenous rights angle; general wildfire and wildlife-service updates not led by or directly affecting Indigenous communities or guardians; provincial forestry and environmental policy with no explicit First Nations involvement; consumer tech and gadget reviews; science with no Indigenous stewardship or sovereignty context; crime and judicial news unrelated to Indigenous rights.

CALIBRATION — apply this ladder to everything else. Indigenous-led journalism on governance, rights, and self-determination is a strong fit on its own: a technology hook raises a score but is NOT required to reach the top band.
- 80-100: Excellent Indigenous-led reporting. Cariboo stories bridging governance or culture AND technology land here (Tŝilhqot'in/Secwépemc/Dakelh language revitalization tech, guardian programs using sensors and drones, GIS land mapping, Indigenous-led connectivity, digital heritage projects) — and so does outstanding national coverage of sovereignty, treaty, and land rights.
- 55-79: Solid pan-Canadian Indigenous governance, sovereignty, land rights, treaty, or reconciliation journalism — APTN, Eagle Feather News, or IndigiNews-style coverage of First Nations governance, MMIWG, land claims, self-determination, and Indigenous-led services. Most Indigenous governance journalism belongs HERE, not below.
- 30-54: Indigenous cultural, community, or human-interest stories (awards, events, ceremonies) with limited governance substance, or BC land-stewardship and environmental stories with meaningful First Nations involvement.
- 10-29: General BC land, environmental, or forestry stories that mention Indigenous communities only in passing.

ANCHORS: 'Tŝilhqot'in Nation launches drone-based caribou monitoring on title lands' → 98. 'First Nations leaders reject BC's revised land-title framework' → 75. 'Secwépemc language app reaches 1,000 learners' → 88. 'BC Wildfire Service updates evacuation alerts for the Interior' → 8.

Score 0-100 where 100 is a perfect thematic match and 0 is completely unrelated.

In June, Ahmadi, 29, and eight members of her production team, including musicians, were sentenced by a court in the city of Qom over a concert that was streamed online in 2024, which went viral and racked up millions of views. The court said the group had violated the country’s “legal and cultural norms” and called the performance “obscene and vulgar”.

items.title: [Fast Company] Measles outbreaks surge to top 3,500 cases this year: These tracker maps show the areas hardest hit
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

The United States has reached an ignominious milestone this week.

According to data from the International Vaccine Access Center at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, measles cases have now surpassed the 3,500 mark—a level not seen in 35 years.

Here’s what you need to know about the multiple outbreaks affecting the country, and which areas are currently being hit the hardest.

What’s happened?

According to the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, as of September 18, 3,568 measles cases were reported in the United States this year so far.

More worryingly, nearly 10% of those cases—341 of them—occurred in the previous two weeks leading up to September 18.

The figure is nearly 1,300 more than the total U.S. measles cases reported in all of 2025, and a level not seen since 1991, when the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) says measles cases reached 9,643.

Speaking of those CDC numbers, if you look at the agency’s official data up to September 18, you’ll see it differs slightly from the John Hopkins’s data. According to the CDC, measles cases for 2026 in the U.S. stand at 3,471 as of September 18. That’s a discrepancy of 97.

The difference seems to stem from the timeframes and the data the CDC uses to update its official measles dashboard, including, as the Guardian noted, how it registers measles deaths.

The CDC says its dashboard is updated with “only confirmed measles cases notified to CDC as of noon on Thursdays,” while John Hopkins updates its dashboard on Fridays “with intermittent updates as warranted.”

Why is measles surging in the United States?

Regardless of which current tally you go by, there’s no disputing that measles is running rampant in America compared to the historic number of cases going back the last three decades.

Measles was officially declared eradicated in America in 2000, with only dozens to a few hundred cases popping up in most years between 2000 and 2018. But then in 2019, measles cases spiked to more than 1,200, according to CDC data. 

Cases dropped again during the pandemic as social distancing made the spread of the virus harder, but then in 2025 they surged to nearly 2,300, and in 2026, cases now top 3,500.

And it’s not just America. As reported by UNICEF USA last November, measles cases are rising globally.

But why? UNICEF says there are two main culprits: rising vaccine hesitancy and public health funding cuts. Both have accelerated in the U.S. since 2025, when measles cases began skyrocketing in the country.

Mapping measles in the U.S.

Both the CDC and John Hopkins have maps that track the number of measles cases across the country.

The CDC’s most recent map shows that in 2026, measles cases have been reported in all but five states.

The five states with no reported cases are Arkansas, Hawaii, Mississippi, Nevada, and New Hampshire.

But those are the outliers. The map shows that nine states have reported more than 100 cases each, with the top three states reporting more than 500 cases each.

The worst state when it comes to the number of cases is Pennsylvania, where an outbreak is ongoing. That state so far has had 745 cases in 2026. South Carolina comes in second with 670 cases this year, and Utah third with 527 cases.

John Hopkins’s measles tracker map corroborates those state rankings on a year-to-date basis. However, the university also offers another map that covers just the last two-week period, which helps to visualize where outbreaks are currently occurring.

According to that map, for the September 4 to September 18 period, 314 cases have been confirmed, with the majority—193 of them—happening in Pennsylvania. Ohio is the next state with the highest number of cases, at 58. Wisconsin follows in third place with 20 cases.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Rare pregnancy infections may triple the risk of autism
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

A major Swedish study of 3.7 million people has found that rare TORCH infections passed from a pregnant woman to the fetus are linked to much higher risks of autism and intellectual disability later in life. Children with a congenital TORCH infection were about three times more likely to be diagnosed with autism, more than seven times more likely to have an intellectual disability, and up to 30 times more likely to have severe to profound intellectual disability.

items.title: [Fast Company] This tool tells you how fossil fuel emissions actually translate into heat deaths, coral reef damage, and more
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Every new fossil fuel project that comes online will add more climate-warming carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions into our atmosphere. But just reporting how many tonnes (metric tons) of CO2 a new coal or gas facility will produce can still be abstract. 

What does it really mean, for example, that a single coal mine in Australia will generate an estimated 4.7 billion tonnes of emissions over its lifetime? How will those emissions actually, tangibly impact the world and its inhabitants?

A new open-source tool quantifies that impact, translating tonnes of CO2 emissions into measurable damages—like the number of excess heat deaths in Europe, the cost of crop production loss, or how many more coral reef colonies will succumb to bleaching. 

Called the Carbon Impacts Tracer, the tool was created by climate experts at Australia National University and the University of New South Wales, as well as the Australian Research Council Centre of Excellence for the Weather of the 21st Century and the Lethal Humidity Global Council.

The tracer shows how much damage emissions will cause across eight categories:

  • excess deaths in Europe
  • Great Barrier Reef coral loss
  • crop production loss; glacier loss
  • the loss of labor hours
  • how many more people will be exposed to heat stress
  • additional people in poverty
  • “human climate niche,” which refers to the narrow range of temperatures in which humans have historically lived

For example, take that Australian coal mine: the Carmichael coal project.

Select it from a list of scenarios in the Carbon Impacts Tracer, and the tool can tell you that those 4.7 billion tonnes of emissions would cause an estimated 2,628 additional heat-related deaths in Europe. Or those emissions could be quantified as a crop loss equivalent to the annual food supply for 1.62 million people. Or 87.4 million additional coral colonies lost per bleaching event. Or 248,000 more people tipped into extreme poverty. Or 1.9 million people left outside of the human climate niche. 

Though the tool includes multiple Australian projects that users can preselect, it also features a couple of international examples, such as the Bay Du Nord Project, an offshore oil development off the coast of Canada. 

Brought to you by attribution science

The tracer includes company-level scenarios for fossil fuel giants like BP, ExxonMobil, and Shell. It also allows users to enter a custom emissions amount anywhere between 1 million and 10 billion metric tonnes of CO2 equivalent. 

We know that every tonne of carbon dioxide added to the atmosphere increases global warming, which amplifies climate impacts like heat waves, floods, glacier melt, and so on.

But historically, it’s been difficult to say how much damage a certain amount of emissions or a specific fossil fuel project will actually cause. Researchers have been expanding this field, known as attribution science, which helps specify just how big a role climate change plays in specific instances of extreme weather or natural disasters.

By turning emissions into specific heat-related deaths or crop loss figures, the tool’s creators say that it will make both the fossil fuel companies and governments that approve these projects “accountable for the damage they will do.”

“For decades, fossil fuel producers have been able to extract oil, gas, and coal, and emit pollution to the atmosphere with virtual impunity—even as climate change worsens and damages mount,” the creators wrote in a piece published by the University of New South Wales.

“But we are entering a new era of accountability,” they continue. “Now that climate attribution science has come of age, it’s no longer possible to hide behind the argument that a new gas field is just a drop in the ocean. We can now see just how much damage that drop will do to the climate, nature—and to us.”

items.title: [Fast Company] OpenAI is accused of taking dangerous cyber risks for ‘private gain’ in lawsuit over rogue AI agents
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

In what is now one of many known cases, OpenAI’s agents went rogue in July, launching a cyberattack on Hugging Face.

Now, the ChatGPT maker is being sued over that incident and the other attacks that have since come to light—such as its not-so-casual hacking of an Australian national healthcare database. 

Legal Advocates for Safe Science and Technology (LASST), a self-described public interest nonprofit, has sued OpenAI in San Francisco’s Superior Court. 

LASST alleges that OpenAI violated California’s Comprehensive Data Access and Fraud Act (CDAFA) by accessing computer systems without the other party’s authorization.

The suit notes that California doesn’t allow for the defense to argue that “artificial intelligence autonomously caused the harm to the plaintiff.” 

As Tyler Whitmer, founder and CEO of LASST, put it in a statement: “AI companies are building agents that act autonomously making decisions, taking actions, accessing systems, without human direction at every step. California law is very clear: companies cannot escape responsibility for what their agents do.”

Fast Company has reached out to OpenAI for comment.

“Gravity of the harm”

LASST is also alleging that OpenAI is in violation of the Unfair Competition Law’s unfairness prong.

The “conduct is independently unfair because the gravity of the harm it causes vastly outweighs any utility or justification for it, and because the conduct is immoral, unethical, oppressive, and substantially injurious,” the group bluntly states. 

The suit further points to OpenAI’s response to the attacks as an “unfair business practice.”

In late August, the AI startup, which recently delayed what is expected to be one of the largest IPOs in history, issued an open letter that called for every AI company to “make cyber defense an immediate leadership priority.”

It warned that “In the coming months, AI-enabled cyber attacks will become far more widespread and sophisticated as models around the world become increasingly capable.”

LASST alleges this is unfair positioning as OpenAI is responsible for such cyber risks and is taking dangerous measures for “private gain.” 

OpenAI has launched a site dedicated to “misalignments reports and notices,” along with creating a timeline of these dangerous incidents and its responses. The company claims to be working on additional safeguards, among other protections. 

The nonprofit isn’t seeking any monetary damages in the suit—though OpenAI might prefer giving up money to the actual goal: regulation.

LASST has asked for a court order “prohibiting OpenAI’s AI agents from accessing third-party computer systems without permission, and forbidding OpenAI from continuing to employ unsafe AI development practices that threaten serious harm to the public.”

Thompson Center is a postmodern architectural landmark designed by Helmut Jahn and completed in 1985. Commissioned by Illinois Governor James R. Thompson, the building reinterprets the classical state capitol by turning the traditional dome-and-public-plaza concept inside out. Occupying an entire city block in Chicago's Loop, it features a multicolored, curved glass atrium and a sloping, transparent corner entry. Controversial from day one, it has been criticized for poor climate control, high maintenance costs, and structural and leak issues. To restore it rather than demolish it, the company collaborated with Architecture Plus Information (A+I) to design a project that would integrate the building into the urban life of Chicago's Loop.
